data.title: Trump, Putin and Xi to meet in first trilateral meeting between leaders
data.description:
President Trump plans to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week, marking the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three leaders.

Trump will be in Asia for The Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines and the APEC summit in China.

“The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesman, told reporters.

A senior U.S. official said that no agreement is expected to come of the meeting.

“I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries,” the official said, adding that it’s “hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”

The official noted that Iran will also be a topic of discussion but notably said that the president does not intend to discuss Ukraine.

Trump had suggested earlier this month that he would be having a meeting with Putin and Xi, but it hadn’t been confirmed until now.

The last nuclear arms pact between the U.S. and Russia, the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), expired in February. The treaty had been extended for five years under the Biden administration and capped the number of deployed strategic warheads and deployed launchers the U.S. and Russia could have.

New START could not be extended again, so Trump would need to negotiate a new treaty.

“If it expires, it expires. We’ll do a better agreement,” Trump said in January.

data.title: Rubio, off script, leans into inspiring vision for America as 2028 speculation grows
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio promoted an inspirational view of the United States during remarks at a conservative law conference Friday, invoking the image of a country where an ambitious attitude binds Americans — striving toward living up to the founding ideals

Rubio’s off-script remarks, which followed a keynote address during the annual conference of The Federalist Society, provided a window into how a potential presidential campaign may rally voters.

Rubio has dismissed the notion he’s planning to leave the administration early to launch a presidential campaign. But Republican voters are in favor of his running in 2028, with 45 percent rating him as an excellent candidate, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. Vice President Vance was not far behind with 43 percent. 

Rubio was relaxed, joking and encouraging while responding to questions from law students at the Friday evening conference in Washington, D.C. The conservative legal society served as a key pipeline for staffing President Trump’s second term and implementing an expansive view of executive power. 

The secretary encouraged one student to focus on the value of human dignity and caring for the less fortunate when asked how a Christian attorney should respond when pressured to leave faith at the door. 

“Remember, I did land-use and zoning,” Rubio joked of his law practice, moving seamlessly between humor and sincerity — demonstrating skills he’s honed throughout an over two-decade political career. 

On Iran, Rubio said U.S. economic pressure is replacing the need for military action — echoing Trump’s downplaying of renewed strikes on the country — but did not provide a vision for an offramp. 

“It’s hard, it’s not easy, and it’s difficult, and oftentimes it inflicts pain, economic pain, and otherwise. So, we recognize that, but victory is they can never have a nuclear weapon,” he said. 

Rubio gave a lighter touch to hot-button culture issues, where the Trump administration has sought to overhaul how America’s history is presented related to slavery, racism and imperialism. 

“I never said our history’s perfect, I said our history is better than anybody else’s,” Rubio said in response to a question on how to instill “love for the values of our country” for the next generation.

Rubio said, “All the great justice movements in our history” — the end of slavery, segregation and women lacking the right to vote — was a “demand that we live up to our founding principle.”

The secretary’s off-script remarks served as a contrast to a more bullish and confrontational prepared speech, where Rubio accused practitioners of international law of making an effort to weaken the United States — drawing applause when highlighting the administration’s sanctioning of the International Criminal Court. 

“They think they have the right to rule over everyone,” he said. 

“If they are foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees, our answer will be the same as the Roman general Pompey… ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

That line unexpectedly drew laughter, causing the secretary to adlib into a joke about how Pompey was not politically correct. 

The secretary’s prepared remarks on Friday echoed a speech he delivered last month in Athens, where he sought to make a case for America’s unrestrained ambition and right to conquest.

The October speech also drew attention as possibly laying the groundwork for a 2028 presidential run. The scene was stunning — the ancient Acropolis in the background lit by the setting Mediterranean sun. But the speech was overshadowed by a host of controversies engulfing then-U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Trump fired her shortly after Rubio’s remarks, responding to negative press that Guilfoyle sought to trade access to the administration in exchange for cash. 

Rubio poked fun at Democrats’ resounding midterm victory and pledges by the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif), to investigate allegations of corruption and threats to national security. 

“There was a congressman who said we all needed to lawyer up, so here we are,” he quipped.

data.title: Watch: Duffy, Mullin hold press briefing on FAA nationwide ground stop
data.description:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will hold a press briefing at the White House on Friday night to provide an update on the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) nationwide ground stop.

“The @FAANews [FAA] issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Duffy wrote on the social platform X. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The ground stop prevents all flights from taking off from U.S. airports.

Watch live above.

Hegseth directs Pentagon CFO to transform military pay systems

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed the Pentagon’s comptroller to begin a “comprehensive transformation” of the military pay systems, arguing the current process has resulted in a growing backlog of “pay challenges.” 

© Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press

“We’ve always wanted to be higher, and a benefits package as a small sign of our appreciation. Our warriors earn every last penny, and we want to make sure that America’s warriors get all the benefits that they deserve,” Hegseth said in a video posted Friday to the social platform X.

 

Jules “Jay” Hurst III is the Pentagon’s comptroller, who was confirmed by the Senate in early August. 

 

The Defense secretary said the department should not be doing manual tasks at this point and that delayed benefits and payment errors are “unacceptable.” 

 

“That ends today. This is a different department, and our warriors deserve much better,” he said in the 97-second video. “Under the old process, when there was a dispute about the payment, the department actually withheld the usual pay until it was resolved. We’re not doing that anymore.” 

 

Hegseth said the rule now will be that the warfighter is first in principle while the Pentagon figures out what went wrong in the process.

 

“The best troops in the world deserve the best pay system we can provide, especially in a world where you can do anything with a click on an iPhone,” the Pentagon chief said. “That is exactly what this administration will achieve for our warriors starting now.

data.title: Multiple college football teams in flight limbo due to FAA ground stop
data.description:
The nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration Friday afternoon has impacted travel plans for college football teams scheduled to fly to their destinations.

Among teams impacted are four schools in the NCAA’s Big 12 Conference, Baylor University, Kansas State University, University of Utah and Arizona State University; three in the Big Ten — University of Minnesota, Purdue University and University of Washington; as well as the universities of Mississippi, Tennessee and Texas, ESPN reported Friday night.

Teams including Oregon State University, Boise State University, University of North Texas and University of Wyoming were also on flights that were either grounded or never left due to the stop, according to ESPN.

The nationwide grounding began at around 4 p.m. EST and continued into Friday evening. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a 4:16 p.m. post on social platform X made the order “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he added.

The agency shared an attributing the ground stop to “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication of a “nefarious attack” against air travel infrastructure as the federal government continues to conduct its investigation.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage – out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA wrote on social media just after 5 p.m.

“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

data.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirement enforcement
data.description:
The Trump administration is delaying the implementation of controversial Medicaid work requirements, giving states an extra six months to prepare. 

The work requirements, which Republicans established in the One Big Beautiful Bill last year, will still technically go into effect Jan. 1. But states will have an optional “hold harmless” transition period that will run through the end of June, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said Friday. 

States that implement the hold harmless period will assess whether individuals meet the work requirement or are excluded from it, but they will not deny applications or disenroll otherwise eligible individuals solely for failure to meet the requirement, CMS said. 

The delay will also give states an opportunity to learn from the early months of implementation to “identify and address workforce training needs and improve the beneficiary experience,” CMS said. 

Once the requirements are enforced, millions of Americans will have to start proving they work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours per month — or risk getting kicked off their health insurance. 

“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman said in a statement.

“If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it,” he added. “And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go.” 

CMS has been facing pressure from states and Democratic lawmakers to delay the effective date.

States said the implementation was rushed from the start, as the law gave less than 18 months from enactment to go-live date. They said they weren’t given enough time to set up the verification systems needed to enforce the new requirements. 

Advocates said the rushed implementation risked millions more people becoming entangled in paperwork and administrative red tape, and losing coverage. 

According to the Congressional Budget Office, about 5 million fewer people are expected to be enrolled in Medicaid over the next 10 years because of the work requirements; most of those people are expected to be uninsured. 

Last month, a federal judge put more uncertainty into the process when he ruled CMS was too strict when it outlined how people can be considered too “medically frail” to work.  

Democratic-led states had sued CMS over its regulation, charging it went further than what Congress intended.

data.title: House Democrat calls FAA stop 'quite disturbing'
data.description:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) called the nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday “quite disturbing.”

“This is quite disturbing and pretty extraordinary of a action taken,” Garcia said during an appearance on MS NOW. “Whatever it is, I think deserves as much transparency as possible.”

“The impact is going to be immense,” the congressman added.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a post on social platform X that the ground stop was issued “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he added.

The agency shared an advisory citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety” for the ground stop, according to The New York Times. The advisory is not currently listed on the FAA’s website.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage – out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA wrote on social media.

“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Garcia said if it is a “technical issue … then I think we just need to know what that is immediately.”

“The amount of people that are going to be grounded across this country is going to cause major interruptions and chaos,” he added.

data.title: Jeffries outlines Democratic plans for Medicare expansion
data.description:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Friday endorsed efforts to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand the program, as Democrats try to navigate internal tensions around a progressive push for Medicare for All. 

During a conference in Denver about the future of the Democratic party, Jeffries outlined the healthcare legislative priorities Democrats plan to tackle once he takes over as House speaker in January. 

Jeffries said the party must first undo Republican cuts to Medicaid funding and restore the Affordable Care Act’s temporary enhanced premium tax credits that Democrats provided during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

While he stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All, Jeffries said Democrats need to go further than merely restoring what Republicans took. 

“I think we’ve got to lower the age of eligibility as it relates to Medicare. I think we’ve got to make sure that we cover hearing, vision, and dental, and we’ve got to make sure that every child in America can be able to see a doctor with high-quality affordable health care,” Jeffries said. 

“These are steps that we can take.” 

Medicare for All has become a critical issue on the left over the last decade, largely due to the efforts of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)  

Buoyed by the victories of candidates like Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.   

After the election, Sanders called on Democrats to lower the Medicare age to 55 through budget reconciliation, which can pass on a party-line vote, as an “immediate first step” towards Medicare for All. 

Sanders also said Democrats should add dental, vision and hearing coverage to Medicare and expand children’s coverage. 

In Denver Jeffries, who has been criticized by progressive activists for not being bold enough and for being friendly to special interests, was repeatedly heckled by protesters. 

“Medicare for all now!” yelled one.  

“Why should we trust you?” one shouted, while another called Jeffries a “traitor.”  

But unlike his Senate counterpart Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Jeffries faces no serious competition in his bid to be elected House Speaker.  

“Remember y’all, I grew up in Brooklyn,” he said with a smile.

data.title: Fed unveils 2027 calendar, confirming October meeting will not include rates vote
data.description:
The Federal Reserve on Thursday released next year’s schedule for its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), confirming that one meeting will feature discussions on strategy and not a vote on interest rates.

The Fed said in a release the FOMC will meet eight times in 2027, with the first meeting in late January and subsequent meetings at six-week intervals.

On the second and final day of those meetings, the panel will vote on the federal funds rate, with the exception of its gathering on Oct. 26-27 of next year.

That meeting, the Fed said, will be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.”

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced the change last month, after FOMC officials held interest rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. The central bank chair said the committee is making the switch for “straightforward” reasons.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals,” he told reporters. 

“But it’s equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point,” Warsh added.

Warsh raised a change to the FOMC’s schedule during the panel’s July meeting, according to the minutes.

The first-year chair “observed that six scheduled meetings” each year, held every two months, would “allow more information to accumulate between meetings” than under the status quo, the minutes noted.

Warsh said last month he expects for the FOMC to have two meetings dedicated to strategy discussions and six for setting monetary policy in 2028. Under the Federal Reserve Act, the panel must meet at least four times per year.

Jason Furman, the chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under former President Obama, praised Warsh’s tweak to the Fed calendar as a “great move” last month.

“I have long thought the Fed spends too much time on the immediate and not nearly enough time thinking about longer-term strategy,” Furman wrote on social platform X. 

The change marks the latest example of Warsh, who succeeded former Fed Chair Jerome Powell in May, putting his imprint on the central bank.

The FOMC’s policy statements have skewed away from including “forward guidance,” information about the likely future conduct of monetary policy.

Warsh has also been alone among 19 committee officials in not providing a “dot” prediction about future rates decisions for either of the FOMC’s two quarterly economic projections since he took over.

The Fed chair has laid out his preference for limiting future projections throughout his nearly six months in charge, saying in July market participants “are learning to play the ball, not the referee” without them.

“I understand the desire for rolling forecasts and commentary from this committee. But for our part, we need to observe market reaction to developments, direct and unfiltered,” Warsh told reporters at the time.
